title: Data Visualization: The Automation Risk Premium vs. Wage Penalties in Global AI Labor Markets
text:
Does Automation Risk Suppress AI Salaries?
The Industry Divergence and Seniority ShieldAs artificial intelligence transforms technical labor, workers face competing economic forces: an “automation risk premium” that compensates for vulnerability, or a “wage penalty” that depresses earnings in automatable roles. Analyzing 3,952 full-time AI positions from the Global AI Jobs Report reveals a striking puzzle: at the aggregate market level, automation risk and salary distribution exhibit virtually zero correlation (\(r = 0.0005\)). A closer inspection uncovers stark sectoral divergence. In technical infrastructure and enterprise sectors such as Insurance and Cloud Computing, roles facing higher automation exposure command higher salaries, reflecting a compensating risk premium. Conversely, in Research & Development and E-commerce, higher automation risk coincides with lower compensation, demonstrating an observable wage penalty.What explains this fragmentation? Decomposing salaries across experience levels, AI specializations, and company sizes resolves the tension. Automation risk is evenly distributed across seniorities (averaging 22% to 24%), but compensation is dictated by institutional hierarchy. Executive and Lead salaries average $347,618 and $217,453, respectively, dwarfing entry-level wages of $74,202 regardless of automation exposure. Rather than a blanket risk premium or penalty, the AI labor market treats automation risk as background noise: specialized domain seniority provides a robust economic shield, whereas industry-specific capital allocation dictates whether risk is compensated or penalized.

section: Compute industry-level correlations, standard errors, and 95% CIs
text:
Compute industry-level correlations, standard errors, and 95% CIs
industry_stats <- ai_data %>% group_by(Industry) %>% summarize( n = n(), mean_salary = mean(Salary_USD, na.rm = TRUE), median_salary = median(Salary_USD, na.rm = TRUE), mean_risk = mean(Automation_Risk_%, na.rm = TRUE), r = cor(Automation_Risk_%, Salary_USD, use = “complete.obs”), p_val = cor.test(Automation_Risk_%, Salary_USD)$p.value, # Fisher z-transformation for 95% CI of Pearson r z = atanh(r), se_z = 1 / sqrt(n - 3), ci_lower = tanh(z - 1.96 * se_z), ci_upper = tanh(z + 1.96 * se_z), .groups = “drop” ) %>% arrange(r) %>% mutate( Industry = factor(Industry, levels = Industry), Regime = case_when( p_val < 0.05 & r < 0 ~ “Wage Penalty (p < .05)”, p_val < 0.05 & r > 0 ~ “Wage Premium (p < .05)”, TRUE ~ “Statistically Indeterminate” ) ) ##

title: Data Viz
text:
The goal of this assignment is not simply to make several good-looking graphs. Your goal is to use a sequence of visualizations to communicate an empirical story: to guide a reader through a question, pattern, comparison, complication, or resolution in a deliberate order.
A useful test: if your figures could be rearranged in any order without changing the meaning of the presentation, you probably have a collection of plots rather than a data story.
You will then tell the same underlying story twice. The evidence should remain the same, but your design choices, level of technical detail, prose, annotations, and use of interactivity should reflect two different communication settings:

A scientific article
An accessible/dynamic web-based outlet

At least two substantive data visualizations are required in each version.




By completing this assignment, you should be able to:

Identify a clear empirical message in a dataset and organize evidence into a coherent narrative arc.
Create multiple visualizations that perform distinct jobs within that narrative rather than redundantly displaying the same result.
Use R to produce polished, reproducible data visualizations and a rendered web document.
Adapt visualization design and explanatory text to different audiences and publication contexts.
Distinguish scientific precision and technical reporting from public-facing clarity, accessibility, and engagement.
Use Git and GitHub to make the complete analysis reproducible and GitHub Pages to publish the finished work.

title: Data Viz
text:
Version A: Scientific Article
Present your story as though the figures and accompanying text were being prepared for a conventional scientific journal article.
Prioritize precision, interpretability, reproducibility, and technical completeness.
Your scientific version should generally:

Use static figures.
Be fully interpretable in black-and-white or greyscale as is often required by scientific journals. Do not rely on colour to encode essential information.
Use conventional scientific labels, units, scales, legends/direct labels, and figure captions as appropriate.
Report technical information needed to interpret the visualization—for example, sample sizes, uncertainty, model quantities, or definitions where relevant.
Keep decorative elements restrained. The visual hierarchy should emphasize the data and the scientific point.
Use prose appropriate for a scientifically literate reader. Technical terminology is appropriate when it improves precision.

title: Data Viz
text:
Version B: Accessible / Dynamic Outlet
Now present the same empirical story for an audience encountering it through an engaging web article, explainer, or similar public-facing medium.
Prioritize clarity, accessibility, narrative flow, and reader engagement without changing or overstating the evidence.
Your accessible/dynamic version might:

Use plain-language, takeaway-oriented headings and explanatory text.
Use colour, highlighting, direct annotation, icons, small multiples, or other design devices when they help guide attention.
Use interactive or dynamic elements—for example, tooltips, filters, animation, or plotly—when they add genuine explanatory value. Interactivity is cool, but is not required for its own sake.
Reduce unnecessary technical detail in the main visual display while preserving enough context for the claims to be understood accurately.
Make deliberate accessibility choices: readable text, sufficient contrast, sensible colour use, clear labels, and alternatives to colour-only encoding.
Think about pacing. Guide the reader through the evidence rather than confronting them with all available information at once.


Important: Adaptation Is Not Decoration
The two versions should not simply be identical figures with a different ggplot2 theme applied.
Your choices should demonstrate that you understand how audience and medium change what information is foregrounded, how it is explained, and how the reader’s attention is directed, while the underlying empirical claims remain consistent.

title: Data Viz
section: 1. Good Authority: Republicans’ Fascination with Testosterone, in Three Charts
text:
1. Good Authority: Republicans’ Fascination with Testosterone, in Three Charts
https://goodauthority.org/news/republicans-fascination-with-testosterone-in-three-charts/
This is close to the scope of the story expected for this assignment.
Pay particular attention to how three relatively conventional plots become an argument through sequencing. Each visualization answers or develops something raised by the previous one, while the prose explains why the next piece of evidence matters.
Notice that the effectiveness of the piece does not depend on technically elaborate visualizations. The strength comes from deciding:
What should the reader see first? What question does that create? What evidence should they see next?

title: Data Viz
text:
2. The Economist: The Banana Index
Data and materials:
https://github.com/TheEconomist/banana-index-data
This example illustrates how repeating a visual grammar while changing the analytical perspective can itself tell a story.
The comparison changes depending on how the environmental impact of food is evaluated—for example, relative to weight, calories, or protein.
Pay attention to how holding much of the visual form constant makes it easier for the reader to focus on the thing that is changing: the basis of comparison.
This is also an excellent example of making a potentially technical measurement issue intuitive and visually accessible.

title: Data Viz
section: 3. The Pudding: Is the Love Song Dying?

title: Data Viz
text:
Learning from the Exemplars
Do not imitate these examples mechanically.
Instead, use them to study how authors decide:
What does the reader see first?
What question or tension does that create?
What evidence comes next?
How does that evidence change what the reader thinks about the previous visualization?
What should the reader conclude by the end?
That sequence—not simply the number or attractiveness of the plots—is what turns several visualizations into a data story.

text:
Does Automation Risk Suppress AI Salaries?
The Industry Divergence and Seniority ShieldAs artificial intelligence transforms technical labor, workers face competing economic forces: an “automation risk premium” that compensates for vulnerability, or a “wage penalty” that depresses earnings in automatable roles. In technical infrastructure and enterprise sectors such as Insurance and Cloud Computing, roles facing higher automation exposure command higher salaries, reflecting a compensating risk premium. Conversely, in Research & Development and E-commerce, higher automation risk coincides with lower compensation, demonstrating an observable wage penalty.What explains this fragmentation? Decomposing salaries across experience levels, AI specializations, and company sizes resolves the tension. title: Data Visualization: The Automation Risk Premium vs. Wage Penalties in Global AI Labor Markets
text:
Methods

Observations
The analytical dataset is extracted from the Global AI Jobs Report 2026, comprising 5,000 international job postings across 28 industry sectors and 8 artificial intelligence specializations. To eliminate structural confounding arising from non-standard labor contracts, part-time arrangements, and hourly freelance rates, the sample was strictly restricted to verified full-time employment postings (\(N = 3,952\), representing \(79.0\%\) of the initial database).


Measures
Annual Compensation (Salary): Advertised base salary in US Dollars (USD). Across the full-time sample, compensation spans from \(\$27,934\) to \(\$718,357\) (Mean = \(\$157,223\), Median = \(\$140,591\), \(\text{SD} = \$78,578\)). Automation Exposure Index (Auto_Risk): Continuous index measuring task-level automation susceptibility, ranging from \(5.0\%\) to \(40.0\%\) (Mean = \(22.8\%\), Median = \(22.9\%\), \(\text{SD} = 10.1\%\)). Professional Seniority (Experience): Five-level ordinal factor: Entry Level (\(n = 381\)), Mid Level (\(n = 1,143\)), Senior Level (\(n = 1,417\)), Lead Level (\(n = 800\)), and Executive (\(n = 211\)). AI Specialization (Specs): Primary domain expertise across 8 categories: Deep Learning, Generative AI, Reinforcement Learning, Computer Vision, Machine Learning, Robotics, NLP, and Other. Firm Scale (Size): Enterprise headcount classified into Small (1–50), Medium (51–500), Large (501–5,000), and Enterprise (5,000+).


Data Analysis Strategy
Macro-Level Association: Bivariate Pearson product-moment correlation (\(r\)) and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression between Auto_Risk and Salary across the entire pooled full-time cohort (\(N = 3,952\)). Sub-Sector Stratification: Partitioning data across all 28 industries to calculate intra-sector correlations, two-tailed \(p\)-values, Fisher’s \(z\)-transformations, and \(95\%\) confidence intervals:\[z = \text{atanh}(r), \quad \text{SE}_z = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n - 3}}, \quad \text{CI}_z = z \pm 1.96 \cdot \text{SE}_z, \quad \text{CI}_r = \tanh(\text{CI}_z)\] Linear Marginal Rate Estimation: Estimating intra-industry marginal wage effects (\(\Delta\text{Wage} / \Delta\text{Risk}\)) using bivariate regression lines for contrasting focal sectors. Covariate Decomposition: Stratifying compensation across seniority cohorts, specialization domains, and enterprise size tiers to test for structural confounding.

title: Data Visualization: The Automation Risk Premium vs. Wage Penalties in Global AI Labor Markets
text:
Results
Aggregate Market NeutralityAt the macro level, full-time AI roles demonstrate no linear relationship between displacement risk and advertised earnings (\(r = 0.00045, p = 0.977\)). As presented in Figure 1a, the fitted OLS regression line is completely horizontal across the automation risk distribution (\(5\%\text{--}40\%\)).









Sectoral Divergence: Risk Premiums vs. Wage PenaltiesDisaggregating by sector reveals that the flat aggregate trend masks substantial opposing forces. Across 28 industries (Figure 1b), correlation coefficients range from \(r = -0.230\) to \(r = +0.163\).









Two sectors achieve two-tailed statistical significance (\(p < 0.05\)): Research & Development (\(n = 139\)): \(r = -0.230\) (\(95\%\text{ CI } [-0.382, -0.066], p = 0.0065\)), demonstrating an automation wage penalty. Insurance (\(n = 145\)): \(r = +0.163\) (\(95\%\text{ CI } [0.0003, 0.318], p = 0.0497\)), demonstrating an automation risk premium. Figure 1c plots the fitted marginal regressions for these two polar sectors. In Research & Development, each 1 percentage point increase in automation exposure reduces advertised compensation by \(-\$2,046.22\). In Insurance, each 1 percentage point increase yields a \(+\$1,510.77\) compensation gain.
The Seniority Shield and Structural CovariatesDecomposing the labor market across experience tiers resolves why automation risk fails to exert uniform downward pressure. As displayed in Figure 2a, mean automation exposure is invariant across ranks: Entry Level (\(23.2\%\)), Mid Level (\(22.5\%\)), Senior Level (\(22.8\%\)), Lead Level (\(22.9\%\)), and Executive (\(23.8\%\)). In contrast, mean salaries scale by \(468\%\) from Entry Level (\(\$74,202\)) to Executive (\(\$347,618\)).









Furthermore, technical specialization produces minimal wage variance (Figure 2b). Generative AI roles average \(\$160,362\), which is only \(3.4\%\) higher than foundational Machine Learning roles (\(\$155,126\)).









Finally, firm scale exhibits a modest inverted premium (Figure 2c): boutique firms (1–50 employees) offer higher average base cash salaries (\(\$160,734\)) than Enterprise corporations (\(\$156,682\)), reflecting competition against large tech equity compensation packages.

title: Data Visualization: The Automation Risk Premium vs. Wage Penalties in Global AI Labor Markets
text:
Discussion
These empirical findings demonstrate that automation risk does not act as a uniform market-wide wage suppressor. Instead, the relationship is mediated by sector-specific capital dynamics: Compensating Risk Differentials in Legacy Enterprises: In heavily regulated, legacy sectors such as Insurance, high automation risk reflects digital overhaul and modernization. Employers must pay a risk premium (\(+\$1,511/\%\)) to recruit top talent into transformation initiatives where workflow obsolescence is high. Task Substitution in Exploratory Sectors: In Research & Development, automation directly targets repeatable data generation and algorithmic prototyping. High automation scores indicate automatable coding tasks that reduce worker bargaining leverage (\(-\$2,046/\%\)). Institutional Dominance of Seniority: The stability of automation risk across experience levels (\(22.5\%\text{--}23.8\%\)) confirms that technical leadership is as exposed to AI-augmented workflows as junior developers. However, institutional decision-making authority creates an economic buffer: senior professionals retain high compensation regardless of task-level displacement vulnerability.

title: Data Visualization: The Automation Risk Premium vs. Wage Penalties in Global AI Labor Markets
text:
Computational Pipeline & Setup
The code block below handles all data ingestion, filtering, statistical modeling, and plot rendering in one place. All figure objects are stored in memory and recalled inside the narrative sections below without cluttering the reading flow.
#| code-summary: “Click to expand the complete data pipeline and visualization code”


1. Load required libraries
library(tidyverse) library(readxl) library(gt) library(scales)


2. Ingest raw data
ai_data <- read_csv(“global_ai_jobs_2026.csv”)


3. Clean and filter data for full-time technical roles
ai_data_clean <- ai_data |> filter(Job_Type == “Full-time”) |> rename( Salary = Salary_USD, Auto_Risk = Automation_Risk_%, Experience = Experience_Level, Specs = AI_Specialization, Size = Company_Size ) |> mutate( Experience = factor( Experience, levels = c(“Entry Level”, “Mid Level”, “Senior Level”, “Lead Level”, “Executive”) ), Size = factor( Size, levels = c(“Small (1-50)”, “Medium (51-500)”, “Large (501-5000)”, “Enterprise (5000+)”) ) ) |> select(Salary, Auto_Risk, Experience, Specs, Industry, Size)


4. Compute industry-level correlations, standard errors, and 95% CIs
industry_stats <- ai_data_clean |> group_by(Industry) |> summarize( n = n(), mean_salary = mean(Salary, na.rm = TRUE), median_salary = median(Salary, na.rm = TRUE), mean_risk = mean(Auto_Risk, na.rm = TRUE), r = cor(Auto_Risk, Salary, use = “complete.obs”), p_val = cor.test(Auto_Risk, Salary)$p.value, z = atanh(r), se_z = 1 / sqrt(n - 3), ci_lower = tanh(z - 1.96 * se_z), ci_upper = tanh(z + 1.96 * se_z), .groups = “drop” ) |> arrange(r) |> mutate( Industry = factor(Industry, levels = Industry), Regime = case_when( p_val < 0.05 & r < 0 ~ “Wage Penalty (p < .05)”, p_val < 0.05 & r > 0 ~ “Wage Premium (p < .05)”, TRUE ~ “Statistically Unclear” ) )


5. Build Scientific Figures (Version A)


Fig 1a: Aggregate market neutrality
fig1a_scientific <- ai_data_clean |> ggplot(aes(x = Auto_Risk, y = Salary)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.2, shape = 1) + geom_smooth(method = “lm”, formula = y ~ x, color = “black”, linewidth = 0.8, se = TRUE) + scale_y_continuous( labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = “k”), breaks = seq(0, 600000, by = 200000) ) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(5, 40, by = 10)) + labs( title = “Figure 1a. Correlation between Annual Salary and Automation Risk”, subtitle = “Points represent individual job listings; shaded regions depict 95% confidence bounds (N = 3,952).”, x = “Automation Risk Index (%)”, y = “Annual Salary (USD in Thousands)” ) + theme_bw(base_size = 10) + theme( plot.title = element_text(face = “bold”, size = 11), strip.background = element_rect(fill = “grey95”), strip.text = element_text(face = “bold”, size = 9), panel.grid.minor = element_blank() )


Fig 1b: Sectoral forest plot
fig1b_scientific <- ggplot(industry_stats, aes(x = r, y = Industry)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = “dashed”, color = “grey30”, linewidth = 0.5) + geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ci_lower, xmax = ci_upper), width = 0.25, color = “black”, linewidth = 0.5) + geom_point(aes(shape = (p_val < 0.05)), size = 2, fill = “black”) + scale_shape_manual( name = “Significance”, values = c(“TRUE” = 16, “FALSE” = 1), labels = c(“TRUE” = “p < 0.05”, “FALSE” = “p >= 0.05”) ) + scale_x_continuous( limits = c(-0.45, 0.45), breaks = seq(-0.4, 0.4, by = 0.1), labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1) ) + labs( title = “Figure 1b. Sector-Specific Correlation Between Automation Risk and Compensation”, subtitle = expression(paste(“Pearson correlation coefficients (”, italic(“r”), “) with 95% confidence intervals across 28 industries (”, italic(“N”), ” = 3,952).”)), x = expression(paste(“Correlation Coefficient (”, italic(“r”), “)”)), y = “Industry Sector”, caption = “Note: Solid markers denote statistical significance at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed test).” ) + theme_classic(base_size = 10) + theme( plot.title = element_text(face = “bold”, size = 11, hjust = 0), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, margin = margin(b = 8)), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8), legend.position = “bottom”, panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = “grey90”, linewidth = 0.3) )


Fig 1c: Contrasting regression slopes for focal industries
focal_industries <- c(“Research & Development”, “Insurance”) fig1c_scientific <- ai_data_clean |> filter(Industry %in% focal_industries) |> mutate(Industry = factor(Industry, levels = focal_industries)) |> ggplot(aes(x = Auto_Risk, y = Salary)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.2, shape = 1) + geom_smooth(method = “lm”, formula = y ~ x, color = “black”, linewidth = 0.8, se = TRUE) + facet_wrap(~ Industry, ncol = 2, scales = “fixed”) + scale_y_continuous( labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = “k”), breaks = seq(0, 600000, by = 200000) ) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(5, 40, by = 10)) + labs( title = “Figure 1c. Linear Marginal Effects of Automation Risk on Compensation”, subtitle = “Points represent individual job listings; shaded regions depict 95% confidence bounds.”, x = “Automation Risk Index (%)”, y = “Annual Salary (USD in Thousands)” ) + theme_bw(base_size = 10) + theme( plot.title = element_text(face = “bold”, size = 11), strip.background = element_rect(fill = “grey95”), strip.text = element_text(face = “bold”, size = 9), panel.grid.minor = element_blank() )


Fig 2a: The seniority shield
seniority <- ai_data_clean |> group_by(Experience) |> summarize( mean_salary = mean(Salary, na.rm = TRUE), mean_risk = mean(Auto_Risk, na.rm = TRUE), n = n() )
fig2a_scientific <- ggplot(seniority, aes(x = Experience, y = mean_salary)) + geom_col(fill = “#37474F”, width = 0.55) + geom_text( aes(label = paste0(dollar(round(mean_salary)), “(Risk:”, round(mean_risk, 1), “%)”)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3.2 ) + scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format(), limits = c(0, 400000)) + labs( title = “Figure 2a. The Seniority Shield (Compensation for Automation Risk)”, subtitle = “Salaries increase 4.7x across ranks, while automation exposure remains static at ~23%.”, x = “Experience Level”, y = “Average Annual Salary (USD)”, caption = “Full-time positions (N = 3,952). Mean automation risk is annotated above each tier.” ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())


Fig 2b: Specialization parity
spec_summary <- ai_data_clean |> group_by(Specs) |> summarize( mean_salary = mean(Salary, na.rm = TRUE), mean_risk = mean(Auto_Risk, na.rm = TRUE), n = n() ) |> arrange(desc(mean_salary))
fig2b_scientific <- ggplot(spec_summary, aes(x = reorder(Specs, mean_salary), y = mean_salary)) + geom_point(size = 4, color = “#00838F”) + geom_segment(aes(x = Specs, xend = Specs, y = 140000, yend = mean_salary), color = “grey60”) + coord_flip() + scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format(), limits = c(140000, 170000)) + labs( title = “Figure 2b. Compensation Parity Across AI Disciplines”, subtitle = “Generative AI ($160k) offers no substantial wage premium over Computer Vision ($159k) or Machine Learning ($155k).”, x = “AI Specialization”, y = “Average Salary (USD)”, caption = “Baseline truncated at $140k to highlight discipline dispersion.” ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())


Fig 2c: Company size dynamics
size_summary <- ai_data_clean |> group_by(Size) |> summarize( mean_salary = mean(Salary, na.rm = TRUE), median_salary = median(Salary, na.rm = TRUE), n = n() )
fig2c_scientific <- ggplot(size_summary, aes(x = Size, y = mean_salary)) + geom_col(fill = “#5D4037”, width = 0.5) + geom_text(aes(label = dollar(round(mean_salary))), vjust = 1.5, color = “white”, fontface = “bold”, size = 3.5) + scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format()) + labs( title = “Figure 2c. Small Startups Pay Higher Base Cash Salaries”, subtitle = “Boutique firms (1-50 employees) offer $160.7k on average to compete against Enterprise giants ($156.7k).”, x = “Firm Headcount Tier”, y = “Mean Base Salary (USD)”, caption = “N = 3,952 full-time AI jobs.” ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

Story Summary Does automation risk depress wages for the engineers developing artificial intelligence? Standard economic theory offers two competing hypotheses: a compensating risk premium (firms pay more to attract talent to automatable roles) or an automation wage penalty (task displacement erodes worker bargaining power). Analyzing 3,952 full-time AI positions from the Global AI Jobs Report 2026 reveals an aggregate puzzle: at the macro level, automation risk and salary exhibit virtually zero correlation (\(r = 0.0005\)). Disaggregating the data by industry uncovers a deep structural divide. Capital-intensive enterprise sectors like Insurance (\(r = +0.16\), \(+\$1,511\) per risk percentage point) and Cloud Computing (\(r = +0.13\), \(+\$1,099/\%\)) offer substantial automation risk premiums. Conversely, Research & Development (\(r = -0.23\), \(-\$2,046/\%\)) and E-commerce (\(r = -0.16\), \(-\$1,344/\%\)) impose sharp wage penalties.Investigating overlooked structural covariates resolves this paradox. Automation risk is evenly distributed across career stages (averaging \(22.5\%\text{--}23.8\%\)), yet compensation is dictated by organizational hierarchy: Executive salaries average \(\$347,618\) compared to \(\$74,202\) for entry-level workers. Furthermore, technical specialization yields negligible wage differentials (Generative AI commands \(\$160\text{k}\) versus classical Machine Learning at \(\$155\text{k}\)), while national geography creates wage disparities exceeding \(130\%\). Automation risk does not inherently suppress AI earnings; its wage effect is mediated by industry business models, while professional seniority provides a durable economic shield.2. title: Data Visualization: The Automation Risk Premium vs. Wage Penalties in Global AI Labor Markets
text: The Industry Divergence and Seniority ShieldAs artificial intelligence transforms technical labor, workers face competing economic forces: an “automation risk premium” that compensates for vulnerability, or a “wage penalty” that depresses earnings in automatable roles. Analyzing 3,952 full-time AI positions from the Global AI Jobs Report reveals a striking puzzle: at the aggregate market level, automation risk and salary distribution exhibit virtually zero correlation (\(r = 0.0005\)). A closer inspection uncovers stark sectoral divergence. In technical infrastructure and enterprise sectors such as Insurance and Cloud Computing, roles facing higher automation exposure command higher salaries, reflecting a compensating risk premium. Conversely, in Research & Development and E-commerce, higher automation risk coincides with lower compensation, demonstrating an observable wage penalty.What explains this fragmentation? Decomposing salaries across experience levels, AI specializations, and company sizes resolves the tension. Automation risk is evenly distributed across seniorities (averaging 22% to 24%), but compensation is dictated by institutional hierarchy. Executive and Lead salaries average $347,618 and $217,453, respectively, dwarfing entry-level wages of $74,202 regardless of automation exposure. Rather than a blanket risk premium or penalty, the AI labor market treats automation risk as background noise: specialized domain seniority provides a robust economic shield, whereas industry-specific capital allocation dictates whether risk is compensated or penalized.

title: Data Visualization: The Automation Risk Premium vs. Wage Penalties in Global AI Labor Markets
text:
Does Automation Risk Suppress AI Salaries?
The Industry Divergence and Seniority ShieldAs artificial intelligence transforms technical labor, workers face competing economic forces: an “automation risk premium” that compensates for vulnerability, or a “wage penalty” that depresses earnings in automatable roles. Analyzing 3,952 full-time AI positions from the Global AI Jobs Report reveals a striking puzzle: at the aggregate market level, automation risk and salary distribution exhibit virtually zero correlation (\(r = 0.0005\)). A closer inspection uncovers stark sectoral divergence. In technical infrastructure and enterprise sectors such as Insurance and Cloud Computing, roles facing higher automation exposure command higher salaries, reflecting a compensating risk premium. Conversely, in Research & Development and E-commerce, higher automation risk coincides with lower compensation, demonstrating an observable wage penalty.What explains this fragmentation? Decomposing salaries across experience levels, AI specializations, and company sizes resolves the tension. Automation risk is evenly distributed across seniorities (averaging 22% to 24%), but compensation is dictated by institutional hierarchy. Executive and Lead salaries average $347,618 and $217,453, respectively, dwarfing entry-level wages of $74,202 regardless of automation exposure. Rather than a blanket risk premium or penalty, the AI labor market treats automation risk as background noise: specialized domain seniority provides a robust economic shield, whereas industry-specific capital allocation dictates whether risk is compensated or penalized.

title: Data Visualization: The Automation Risk Premium vs. Wage Penalties in Global AI Labor Markets
text:
Methods

Observations
The analytical dataset is extracted from the Global AI Jobs Report 2026, comprising 5,000 international job postings across 28 industry sectors and 8 artificial intelligence specializations. To eliminate structural confounding arising from non-standard labor contracts, part-time arrangements, and hourly freelance rates, the sample was strictly restricted to verified full-time employment postings (\(N = 3,952\), representing \(79.0\%\) of the initial database).


Measures
Annual Compensation (Salary): Advertised base salary in US Dollars (USD). Across the full-time sample, compensation spans from \(\$27,934\) to \(\$718,357\) (Mean = \(\$157,223\), Median = \(\$140,591\), \(\text{SD} = \$78,578\)).
Automation Exposure Index (Auto_Risk): Continuous index measuring task-level automation susceptibility, ranging from \(5.0\%\) to \(40.0\%\) (Mean = \(22.8\%\), Median = \(22.9\%\), \(\text{SD} = 10.1\%\)).
Professional Seniority (Experience): Five-level ordinal factor: Entry Level (\(n = 381\)), Mid Level (\(n = 1,143\)), Senior Level (\(n = 1,417\)), Lead Level (\(n = 800\)), and Executive (\(n = 211\)).
AI Specialization (Specs): Primary domain expertise across 8 categories: Deep Learning, Generative AI, Reinforcement Learning, Computer Vision, Machine Learning, Robotics, NLP, and Other. Firm Scale (Size): Enterprise headcount classified into Small (1–50), Medium (51–500), Large (501–5,000), and Enterprise (5,000+).


Data Analysis Strategy
Macro-Level Association: Bivariate Pearson product-moment correlation (\(r\)) and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression between Auto_Risk and Salary across the entire pooled full-time cohort (\(N = 3,952\)). Sub-Sector Stratification: Partitioning data across all 28 industries to calculate intra-sector correlations, two-tailed \(p\)-values, Fisher’s \(z\)-transformations, and \(95\%\) confidence intervals:\[z = \text{atanh}(r), \quad \text{SE}_z = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n - 3}}, \quad \text{CI}_z = z \pm 1.96 \cdot \text{SE}_z, \quad \text{CI}_r = \tanh(\text{CI}_z)\]
Linear Marginal Rate Estimation: Estimating intra-industry marginal wage effects (\(\Delta\text{Wage} / \Delta\text{Risk}\)) using bivariate regression lines for contrasting focal sectors. Covariate Decomposition: Stratifying compensation across seniority cohorts, specialization domains, and enterprise size tiers to test for structural confounding.

title: Data Visualization: The Automation Risk Premium vs. Wage Penalties in Global AI Labor Markets
text:
Results
Aggregate Market NeutralityAt the macro level, full-time AI roles demonstrate no linear relationship between displacement risk and advertised earnings (\(r = 0.00045, p = 0.977\)). As presented in Figure 1a, the fitted OLS regression line is completely horizontal across the automation risk distribution (\(5\%\text{--}40\%\)).









Sectoral Divergence: Risk Premiums vs. Wage PenaltiesDisaggregating by sector reveals that the flat aggregate trend masks substantial opposing forces. Across 28 industries (Figure 1b), correlation coefficients range from \(r = -0.230\) to \(r = +0.163\).









Two sectors achieve two-tailed statistical significance (\(p < 0.05\)): Research & Development (\(n = 139\)): \(r = -0.230\) (\(95\%\text{ CI } [-0.382, -0.066], p = 0.0065\)), demonstrating an automation wage penalty. Insurance (\(n = 145\)): \(r = +0.163\) (\(95\%\text{ CI } [0.0003, 0.318], p = 0.0497\)), demonstrating an automation risk premium. Figure 1c plots the fitted marginal regressions for these two polar sectors. In Research & Development, each 1 percentage point increase in automation exposure reduces advertised compensation by \(-\$2,046.22\). In Insurance, each 1 percentage point increase yields a \(+\$1,510.77\) compensation gain.









The Seniority Shield and Structural CovariatesDecomposing the labor market across experience tiers resolves why automation risk fails to exert uniform downward pressure. As displayed in Figure 2a, mean automation exposure is invariant across ranks: Entry Level (\(23.2\%\)), Mid Level (\(22.5\%\)), Senior Level (\(22.8\%\)), Lead Level (\(22.9\%\)), and Executive (\(23.8\%\)). In contrast, mean salaries scale by \(468\%\) from Entry Level (\(\$74,202\)) to Executive (\(\$347,618\)).









Furthermore, technical specialization produces minimal wage variance (Figure 2b). Generative AI roles average \(\$160,362\), which is only \(3.4\%\) higher than foundational Machine Learning roles (\(\$155,126\)).









Finally, firm scale exhibits a modest inverted premium (Figure 2c): boutique firms (1–50 employees) offer higher average base cash salaries (\(\$160,734\)) than Enterprise corporations (\(\$156,682\)), reflecting competition against large tech equity compensation packages.

title: Data Visualization: The Automation Risk Premium vs. Wage Penalties in Global AI Labor Markets
text:
Discussion
These empirical findings demonstrate that automation risk does not act as a uniform market-wide wage suppressor. Instead, the relationship is mediated by sector-specific capital dynamics: Compensating Risk Differentials in Legacy Enterprises: In heavily regulated, legacy sectors such as Insurance, high automation risk reflects digital overhaul and modernization. Employers must pay a risk premium (\(+\$1,511/\%\)) to recruit top talent into transformation initiatives where workflow obsolescence is high. Task Substitution in Exploratory Sectors: In Research & Development, automation directly targets repeatable data generation and algorithmic prototyping. High automation scores indicate automatable coding tasks that reduce worker bargaining leverage (\(-\$2,046/\%\)). Institutional Dominance of Seniority: The stability of automation risk across experience levels (\(22.5\%\text{--}23.8\%\)) confirms that technical leadership is as exposed to AI-augmented workflows as junior developers. However, institutional decision-making authority creates an economic buffer: senior professionals retain high compensation regardless of task-level displacement vulnerability.

section: The Seniority Shield: Why Experience Trumps Automation
text:
The Seniority Shield: Why Experience Trumps Automation
Why isn’t there a universal salary penalty for automation exposure? Because career seniority dominates everything else.









As shown in Figure 3b, regression lines within every experience tier are completely flat across automation risk levels (\(5\%\text{--}40\%\)). Meanwhile, the pay steps between career stages are massive:Entry Level: \(\$74\text{k}\) averageMid Level: \(\$109\text{k}\) averageSenior Level: \(\$156\text{k}\) averageLead Level: \(\$217\text{k}\) averageExecutive: \(\$348\text{k}\) averageExecutives face virtually identical automation exposure (\(23.8\%\)) as Entry-Level engineers (\(23.2\%\)). However, domain leadership, institutional accountability, and architectural oversight protect senior compensation from task-level displacement.
Analytical Limitations Advertised vs. Total Realized Compensation: Salary records represent advertised base pay and exclude unvested stock options, variable bonuses, and equity compensation, which are common in enterprise tech firms.
Task Substitutability vs. Displacement: The Automation_Risk_% metric quantifies task-level automation potential, not immediate workforce reduction.
Cross-Sectional Structure: The dataset reflects job listings from a single survey period rather than tracking individual worker wage trajectories over time.
